735.bp: The Web is made of networks: who knows whom, which websites link to each other, which products get bought together. Predicting missing connections in these networks—figuring out that two people should be friends, or that two products belong in the same recommendation—is how search engines, product discovery, and collaboration tools get built. The harder the network, the more it matters: millions of nodes means you need speed and must understand hidden cliques and communities without solving the entire puzzle up front.
735.wh: Graph neural networks learn from local neighborhoods but struggle to see the big picture—whether a connection depends on what's happening far away in the network. Transformers can see globally but cost quadratically in memory and time: even a modestly large network becomes impossibly slow. Worse, a black-box prediction that says 'yes, these should connect' teaches us nothing about *why*, which matters when you need to validate or debug recommendations.
735.ap: TGSBM fuses two separate ideas: a old, principled theory called Stochastic Block Models (which say a network is made of invisible clusters, and connections happen more within clusters than between them) with a modern Transformer that attends over the graph. The trick is making the Transformer efficient by only looking at a sparse subset of nodes rather than everyone—like how a manager doesn't need to read every email, just key ones—and by encoding the idea that links form via cluster membership directly into the learning process.
735.ww: The mechanism works because you're encoding *both* the structure that really exists (hidden communities) and the global patterns that matter (which nodes talk to whom at scale), and you're doing it in a way the model can learn to interpret. When you explicitly say 'links happen because nodes belong to communities,' you've given the model a true story to latch onto, not a pure black box. Sparse attention means you're only computing what matters, cutting computation from quadratic to near-linear.
735.po: The result is fast—six times faster training than comparable methods—and interpretable: you can ask 'which community does this person belong to?' and get an answer, not just a score. On standard benchmarks, it ranks as the top performer, meaning it predicts the real missing links that humans verify as correct more often than competitors.

736.bp: On social media, people share photos of each other constantly, often without thinking about whether the person in the photo gave permission or wants it public. Privacy on the Web isn't just a setting you flip; it's a choice humans make dozens of times, shaped by what their friends say. Understanding when a friend's comment 'please don't share that' actually stops someone from posting is the foundation for building platforms that respect privacy at scale.
736.wh: You might guess that negative feedback stops sharing: tell someone 'don't post that' and they won't. Reality is messier. Some people with a history of ignoring privacy norms won't listen. Worse, mixed signals—some people saying yes, others saying no—can create pressure that backfires, making people share *more*. The problem is that human psychology isn't uniform; nudges that work for one person trap another.
736.ap: The study recruited real users, showed them photos of other people, and varied what comments appeared: only discouraging ones, only encouraging ones, a mix of both, or none. Then they measured whether the person shared the photo without consent. They also looked at who the person was—did they have prior incidents of privacy violations? The result: comments work differently depending on context and the person's history.
736.ww: Social pressure is powerful but conditional. When feedback aligns with social norms (everyone agrees the photo is unflattering or private), people listen. But if you've already ignored privacy norms in the past, being told 'don't share' can feel like a challenge, especially if some comments encourage sharing anyway—a mix of signals is effectively no signal. The backfire happens because mixed comments don't clarify the norm; they make the person feel the crowd is torn, which removes social pressure entirely.
736.po: Platforms should not assume all comments reduce sharing. Design recommendation: use comments to *clarify* norms, not to contradict each other. Flag users with past privacy violations and apply stronger safeguards before they post. A single, clear social message ('the person in this photo asked not to be posted') stops sharing across groups; mixed or weak signals do not.

737.bp: Every organization watches event streams: network logs (time, source IP, destination, bytes sent), security alerts, payment transactions. When something goes wrong—a cyber attack, fraud, unusual behavior—it shows up as a pattern in the data. The challenge is finding these patterns in massive, noisy streams where both the timestamp and the details (IP, size, type) matter, but exist in different forms: some are numbers, some are categories.
737.wh: Traditional methods discretize time, turning a continuous stream into buckets (second 1, second 2, etc.), which loses fine-grained timing information and makes 'normal' behavior hard to separate from genuine anomalies. They also force all data into one representation: either treating a category like 'Germany' as a number (wrong mathematically), or converting 3.2 gigabytes into a symbol (information loss). Statistical assumptions matter too: if you assume all continuous values come from a normal bell-curve distribution but they don't, your model makes bad predictions.
737.ap: HeteroComp treats the stream as a continuous mixture of hidden patterns. For each attribute—IP, packet size, time—it infers what kinds of values typically appear together and how they change over time. It uses Gaussian processes (a statistical tool that learns unknown distributions rather than guessing them) to handle continuous values flexibly and handles categorical attributes separately. The result is a decomposition into 'components'—each a latent pattern explaining subsets of observations—and a way to score whether a new event is typical or anomalous.
737.ww: By respecting the natural type of each attribute (time as time, categories as categories, numbers as numbers) and learning their true distributions rather than assuming a specific shape, the model can distinguish real anomalies from noise. A denial-of-service attack shows up as a sudden spike in events from a particular IP that doesn't just break a single feature—it breaks *the whole pattern*, which is easier to catch when each feature is modeled correctly.
737.po: The method finds group anomalies (not just one weird event, but a cluster of related events that together are suspicious) and tracks them over continuous time, so you see the rise and fall of an attack in real time, not discretized into buckets. On network and transaction datasets, it detects known attacks faster and with fewer false alarms than methods that assume all data comes from one distribution.

738.bp: Science and data analysis live in code and notebooks that researchers share, but 'sharing on GitHub' often means the code doesn't actually run when someone else tries it. Reproducing someone else's analysis requires the exact same software versions, the right library, and the knowledge to set it all up. The goal is to make research executable with one click—not because it's convenient, but because reproducible science is trustworthy science.
738.wh: Turning a notebook or script into something truly reproducible is tedious: you must specify exactly which version of Python, NumPy, and every dependency you used; you must structure the repository so the code finds its data and outputs; you must document assumptions buried in your code. Most researchers skip this because it feels bureaucratic, so analyses sit in GitHub repos that others can read but not run.
738.ap: This tutorial teaches the practical workflow: how to use MyBinder (a free service that spins up a temporary computer with your code and runs it in a browser) and the GESIS Methods Hub (a catalog of published, executable methods). You learn to write a requirements file listing exact package versions, structure your repository so Binder knows where to find the entry point (which notebook to run), and test the setup so the build actually works before you publish it.
738.ww: A reproducible method is a gift to future you and to anyone building on your work: they don't waste days debugging cryptic errors or reverse-engineering your environment. By front-loading this work—spending an afternoon on documentation and setup—you make your analysis available to thousands of researchers forever, not buried in a private hard drive or a forgotten GitHub.
738.po: Participants leave with a working, one-click-executable method published in a searchable hub, plus templates and checklists they can reuse for their next project. The immediate payoff: one less barrier for others to cite and build on your work. The long-term payoff: science becomes cumulative and trustworthy rather than a series of isolated, unreproducible claims.

739.bp: The Web is shifting from centralized to peer-to-peer storage: instead of one company's server holding all files, IPFS (a network where anyone can contribute storage) holds them. This is powerful for censorship resistance and resilience, but attackers exploit the same decentralization to host phishing sites—fake login pages that steal credentials—that stay online even after the attacker vanishes. Detecting and stopping these campaigns requires understanding how phishing spreads across a decentralized network.
739.wh: Traditional phishing detection watches web servers and domain names, but IPFS is content-addressed: a file is identified by its hash, not a domain name, so the same fake login page can live on thousands of computers at once. Public gateways (services that let you access IPFS files through your regular browser) add another layer: attackers can route victims through reputable gateways to hide their origin, using the gateway's reputation to evade detection.
739.ap: The team built a monitoring system that watches IPFS traffic and traces which gateways serve which files. Over 11 months, they collected data on 10,489 phishing file hashes and grouped them by similarity into 448 campaigns—sets of related phishing pages serving the same scam. They also mapped which gateways (including ones not in official lists) handle the malicious content, and checked whether blocking a few dominant sources could shut down most of the phishing.
739.ww: Phishing clusters reveal attacker behavior: rather than deploying thousands of isolated pages, attackers reuse the same few designs across many victims, which makes the problem concentrable. By identifying the 69 most common clusters, you can target mitigation: take down those clusters and you disable 80% of the detected phishing. The finding that caching across public gateways amplifies attacks means that reputation systems designed for benign use become force multipliers for abuse.
739.po: The research shows that traditional blocklists are insufficient—80% of detected gateways aren't on public lists anyway. Instead, platforms should monitor cluster patterns and prioritize high-impact campaigns. The data also reveals that decentralized systems need decentralized defense: attacking a few central hubs won't work, but identifying campaign structure can.

740.bp: Recommender systems—the engine that suggests products, movies, or news—increasingly run on large language models that generate explanations and reasons alongside suggestions. These models learn from human behavior online, which often encodes prejudice: men's products are recommended to men, women's to women; certain demographic groups see fewer high-quality items. The challenge is fixing these biases without retraining the entire massive model, which would cost millions in compute.
740.wh: Fixing bias in a traditional model meant retraining from scratch, infeasible for an LLM with billions of parameters. Existing debiasing methods target specific known biases (gender, age) but fail when new biases emerge or when multiple biases co-exist. You can't easily audit what the model learned or remove harmful patterns without understanding the entire training pipeline, which is a black box for most users.
740.ap: FUDLR recasts debiasing as machine unlearning: identifying which training examples caused bias, then removing their influence without full retraining. First, it uses a learned mask to identify bias-prone samples—the mask learns which examples, if removed, improve fairness most. The mask is bias-agnostic, meaning you can swap in different fairness metrics (fix gender bias, then age bias, then group bias) without retraining. Second, it estimates how much each identified sample influenced the model's weights and removes that influence through efficient matrix operations.
740.ww: The mechanism works because bias in recommendations usually traces back to statistical patterns in training data: 'this group bought this product, so recommend it to similar people.' By identifying and down-weighting those samples, you break the pattern without erasing the model's ability to make good recommendations for everyone else. The efficiency comes from estimating influence mathematically rather than retraining—you're surgically removing the problem, not rebuilding from scratch.
740.po: The method improves fairness (reduces recommendation gaps between demographic groups) while keeping recommendation accuracy stable, all without retraining. Experiments show it works across diverse real-world biases—a practical path for platforms to deploy fair LLM recommendations today, not after a six-month retrain cycle.

741.bp: Detecting emotion in text—whether a message is joyful, angry, sad, or fearful—is essential for mental health apps, customer service bots, and content moderation. Modern neural networks trained on examples can do this, but they're black boxes: you can't ask 'why did the model think this was angry?' The goal is to make emotion detection not just accurate but interpretable: what words or patterns signal a specific feeling?
741.wh: Neural models achieve high accuracy but are opaque—the model has learned something about emotion but it's encoded in millions of weights you can't read. Humans know that certain words (exclamation marks, 'love,' curse words) signal emotion, but naively adding these as features can hurt accuracy if the model has already learned better patterns. The tension is between transparency (humans understand the features) and performance (the model's implicit learning).
741.ap: The researchers extracted linguistic patterns from 13 different emotion datasets: looking at which words, punctuation, and sentence structures appear in angry text vs. joyful text vs. other emotions. They then added these explicit features (word counts, presence of punctuation, etc.) as auxiliary inputs to a neural model alongside its usual learned representations. The model learns to weight both the explicit signals and its implicit knowledge.
741.ww: Explicit linguistic features act as a regularizer—they guide the model toward solutions that align with human intuition about emotion. When the model sees 'this is an angry text, and humans marked it as angry because it has curse words and exclamation marks,' it learns a more robust path that generalizes better to new texts. The explicit features also provide a sanity check: if the model disagrees with obvious linguistic signals, you know something went wrong.
741.po: Models enriched with linguistic features improve by up to 2.4 points in accuracy on a standard benchmark, and the improvements generalize across different emotion datasets. More importantly, you can now explain predictions: 'the model flagged this as angry because it contains X linguistic markers that correlate with anger,' which is useful for debugging and for users who need to understand why the system made a decision.

742.bp: Detecting anomalous graphs—abnormal networks like a website designed to steal credentials or a social network compromised by bots—is a security problem. You have examples of normal graphs (regular websites) and a few known anomalies (malicious sites) but the attackers keep evolving: they'll build new malicious sites you've never seen that are slightly different from the known bad ones. The goal is to catch *unseen* anomalies, not just recognize copies of known attacks.
742.wh: Machine learning models overfit to known anomalies: they learn 'if a graph has structure X, it's malicious' and miss malicious graphs with structure Y. Labeled anomalies are scarce, so you can't gather enough examples of every attack type. Normal graphs often have quirky substructures—a weird connection pattern—that aren't actually dangerous but make the model think 'this is suspicious,' leading to false alarms.
742.ap: G-GLAD uses two strategies: First, prompt-based anomaly expansion: take known malicious graph structures and use learnable 'prompts' (additional signals) to simulate variations of them—like asking 'what if the attacker changed this part?' This generates a richer set of anomaly types the model learns to recognize. Second, subgraph-based normality extraction: focus on the essential parts of normal graphs that don't indicate anomaly, filtering out spurious quirks. The filtering uses Information Bottleneck (a principle that says keep only the information that matters for the prediction).
742.ww: By expanding the anomaly space, the model sees more attack variants without needing more labeled data—it generates them mathematically. By extracting only essential normality, the model learns what healthy looks like rather than memorizing random quirks of the training set. Together, these make the model confident it can spot new malicious graphs it's never seen before.
742.po: The framework detects both known and novel anomalies across 10 real-world graph datasets, outperforming methods that just try to memorize known anomalies. On a malicious website detection task, it catches attacks that existing methods miss while maintaining low false-alarm rates on normal websites.

743.bp: Modern language models have shifted to 'matmul-free' computation, replacing standard matrix multiplication with simpler bit-wise operations (operations on individual bits of numbers), which run faster on specialized hardware. BitNetv2, a recent model, uses bit-wise computation but faces a problem: when input values bunch up around zero (a normal distribution), the quantization buckets—the discrete levels you round values to—go unused, so most numbers collapse into a few representable levels, losing information. Hardware accelerators need to exploit this insight for speed.
743.wh: Directly implementing bit-wise operations on specialized hardware (processing-in-memory chips) is inefficient: you need separate circuits for different operations. The Hadamard Transform, a mathematical trick that spreads out clustered values so quantization buckets fill evenly, is essential but expensive to compute. Ideally you'd reuse circuit components between the Hadamard computation and the actual bit-wise multiplication, but the math looks different, so hardware designers build separate pipelines.
743.ap: The insight is that Hadamard computation—a sequence of recursive matrix multiplications—can be implemented using the same low-precision weights (weights that are only -1, 0, or 1) as BitLinear's bit-wise accumulation. By restructuring the Hadamard recursion as a butterfly-shaped tree of adders (addition operations), you can reuse that same tree for accumulating results in BitLinear. One physical circuit does both jobs.
743.ww: Reusing hardware means fewer transistors, less power, less data movement (which is often more expensive than computation). When you have a tree of adders built for one job, using it for both Hadamard flattening and bit-wise accumulation cuts the area roughly in half. The mechanism works because the math underlying both operations—reduction trees and accumulation—is structurally identical.
743.po: A more efficient PIM accelerator that keeps the benefits of BitNetv2's Hadamard Transform (better quantization, higher accuracy) without duplicating hardware. This means faster inference and lower power for bit-wise neural networks, making edge deployment of these models practical on resource-constrained devices.

744.bp: On e-commerce sites, users search in unpredictable ways: 'black shoe women's size 8' could mean a specific shoe or a category; 'quick dinner' might search for recipes or restaurants. The search system must guess the user's true intent and rewrite the query to match products better. LLMs can do this well, but they rewrite every query the same way—treating an easy query (one where the user was clear) the same as a hard one (ambiguous or poorly expressed). The goal is to rewrite queries that way humans would, respecting different difficulty levels.
744.wh: Naive LLM-based rewriting treats all queries uniformly, ignoring why rewriting is needed. Some queries need minor tweaks (typo correction); others need semantic restructuring (inferring that 'quick meal delivery' means fast-food restaurants, not a recipe). Without understanding the underlying problem in the query, the model makes misguided rewrites that deviate from human expectations.
744.ap: AWHCP introduces the PIFR paradigm: for each query, identify the Problem (what's unclear?), the Intention (what does the user really want?), the Fix (how should we address it?), and the Rewrite (the final query). The model is fine-tuned on human examples following this structure, learning to reason about difficulty. Then, during inference, the model generates multiple rewrite candidates, and a preference learning stage (using system-side feedback—which rewrites led to successful purchases?) refines the model to prefer rewrites that actually help users find products.
744.ww: By making the model decompose the problem before rewriting, you guide it toward human-like reasoning: 'the user said X but meant Y because Z, so I'll rewrite it this way.' The multi-stage pipeline (supervised learning on PIFR examples, then preference alignment using purchase feedback) teaches the model both how humans think about rewrites and what rewrites actually work in practice.
744.po: Queries rewritten by AWHCP lead to more successful product discovery than baselines, because the rewrites match human reasoning. On e-commerce platforms, this translates to better search, fewer frustrated users, and higher conversion rates because users find what they're looking for faster.

745.bp: Web tables—spreadsheets, data tables on Wikipedia, structured data in research papers—are everywhere, but searching through them is hard. A text search for 'Olympic gold medalists' might miss tables with exactly that data because the table's structure compresses information: the cell values alone don't capture 'this column is country names.' To find the right table, you need embeddings (mathematical summaries of meaning) that capture both the raw content and the structure.
745.wh: Standard embedding models trained on text don't handle tables well: they compress the structured information too much, missing what makes a table useful. Generating lots of examples to train a table-specific model is expensive. Some solutions generate synthetic query examples from tables to improve search, but they arbitrarily pick which columns to include (a partial table), missing opportunities to capture the table's full semantic diversity.
745.ap: CGPT uses K-means clustering to group similar tables, then samples across clusters to create training data that covers the semantic spectrum. For each partial table (subset of rows and columns), an LLM generates synthetic queries, which are used to fine-tune an embedding model. The fine-tuning uses contrastive learning: penalize the model when a query's embedding is far from the matching table's embedding, and reward it when they're close. Over time, the model learns to embed queries and tables so similar ones are nearby.
745.ww: Clustering ensures you don't just train on one type of table—you get diverse examples from the semantic space. LLM-generated queries are diverse and realistic (an LLM trained on real searches knows what people actually ask). Contrastive training is efficient: you're not retraining the entire embedding model from scratch, just refining it to handle table-specific patterns better.
745.po: Tables are found more often with higher precision (16.5% improvement in ranking), and the model generalizes to new types of tables without retraining. This means better table search across Wikipedia, research databases, and knowledge bases—users find data tables as easily as they find documents.

746.bp: Traffic prediction is essential for navigation apps, traffic management, and urban planning: if you can predict congestion five minutes ahead, you can reroute drivers or adjust signal timing. But traffic depends on multiple invisible factors: road networks (which roads connect where), weather, events (concerts, accidents), time of day. A model that only looks at historical traffic patterns misses these factors and makes brittle predictions.
746.wh: Traditional approaches use only historical traffic flow data—ignoring that a concert on tonight and snow on the roads both cause patterns that don't exist in past data. Satellite imagery (geo-images) contains this contextual information, but most models treat imagery as a black box or use it separately from traffic data, missing the interactions. The challenge is fusing different types of information (numbers, images) coherently.
746.ap: VisionST jointly encodes traffic flow patterns and geo-images (satellite photos of the road network and surroundings). First, it extracts visual tokens from satellite imagery—patches of the image that represent nodes in the traffic network or relationships between nodes. Then it generates pattern representations that mix visual signals (what does this area look like?), spatial structure (which roads connect here?), and temporal trends (is this time of day usually congested?). The three perspectives are combined into a unified prediction.
746.ww: By grounding the traffic prediction in what the road actually looks like and what's around it, the model has external context that's not just embedded in historical patterns. A concert venue shows up as a landmark in the image and a spike in past traffic; together, these signal 'today is like concert days.' The integration handles complex, overlapping patterns because all the information—visual, spatial, temporal—is encoded in the same representation space.
746.po: Traffic predictions are more accurate, especially for unusual events or conditions not well-represented in history. Navigation systems using VisionST can warn drivers earlier about congestion and route planning improves, reducing travel time and emissions. The model also generalizes: knowledge learned from one city's traffic patterns transfers to new cities if their road layouts are similar.

747.bp: Detecting anomalous nodes in graphs—finding the compromised account in a social network, the fraud ring in a transaction graph, the infected computer in a network—is crucial for security. Currently, each type of graph (social networks, financial networks, communication networks) requires its own specialized detection model trained on that specific data. If a bank's dataset is different from a telecom company's, you can't reuse the model, which is wasteful and costly.
747.wh: Graphs vary wildly in their structure and node features: social networks have user profiles; financial networks have transaction amounts; security logs have IP addresses and protocols. A model trained on one domain fails on another because it has memorized patterns specific to that data. Getting labeled anomalies for training is hard—breaches are rare—so you can't gather diverse examples. The ideal would be a foundation model for anomaly detection, but graphs are topological and most general models are not.
747.ap: TFM4GAD bridges the gap by flattening graphs into tables that modern tabular foundation models (TFMs) can process. For each node, it computes a rich feature vector: the original node features plus structural summary (Laplacian eigenvalues, which describe the graph's local geometry), neighborhood statistics (what do my neighbors look like?), and anomaly-sensitive aggregations (do my neighbors connect to each other, or just to me?). This augmented table is then fed to a TFM, which uses pre-training and in-context learning to generalize across domains.
747.ww: Tabular models excel at handling missing data, domain shift, and limited labels—precisely the challenges of graph anomaly detection. By computing informative structural features, you translate 'understanding graph structure' into a table-reading problem a TFM knows how to solve. The Laplacian and local statistics capture the essence of graph topology without requiring the model to learn graph neural operations.
747.po: A single model detects anomalies across different types of graphs—social networks, web graphs, transaction networks—without retraining, reducing deployment costs and improving generalization. On benchmark datasets, the approach matches or beats specialized graph models while requiring no labeled data for fine-tuning in new domains.

748.bp: LLMs are increasingly used to moderate content online, deciding whether a message is toxic or hate speech and should be removed. But LLM decisions aren't neutral: they judge implicit hate—subtle language that demeans a group—differently depending on the demographic group mentioned. 'This politician is terrible' is criticism; 'Members of this ethnicity are terrible' is hate speech; but LLMs sometimes misjudge the context, especially for minority groups. Fairness requires consistent, accurate judgments across all demographics.
748.wh: Standard toxicity detection trains a model to classify toxic vs. safe, but inconsistency emerges at inference time: the model handles explicit slurs reliably but struggles with coded language and implicit bias. You can't fully correct this by retraining because the problem is subtle—it requires context the model sometimes misses. Existing approaches try to fix the model via parameter updates, which are expensive and risky for deployed LLMs.
748.ap: FairToT works at inference time: when presented with text to judge, it first detects cases where demographic variation is likely (e.g., statements mentioning a specific group). For these high-risk cases, it applies additional assessment steps using prompts designed to elicit fair, consistent reasoning. It also tracks interpretable fairness indicators—simple metrics that flag inconsistencies—without modifying the model's parameters.
748.ww: Inference-time correction is practical: you don't need to retrain the LLM, just wrap its output with a fairness layer. By identifying risky cases where bias often emerges and applying targeted assessment, you concentrate effort where it matters. Interpretable indicators let you audit fairness: if the model suddenly treats one group harshly, the metrics catch it before deployment.
748.po: Toxicity judgments are fair across demographic groups—group-level disparities shrink—while maintaining accuracy on genuinely toxic content. This means content moderation systems using LLMs can be deployed at scale without perpetuating algorithmic bias. The inference-time approach is practical for platforms: ship the same LLM, add a fairness layer, and improve fairness without expensive retraining.

749.bp: Cameras record security footage constantly: robbery, assault, accidents. When something dangerous happens, we need to know not just that it happened, but *why*: what provoked the attacker? What sequence of events led to the injury? Understanding causality and threat attribution helps security teams prioritize response and helps with investigation and prevention. The goal is automated video understanding that goes beyond detection to explanation.
749.wh: Existing video anomaly detection finds the frame where bad things happen but doesn't explain them. Understanding requires tracking multiple levels of information simultaneously: human body positions and movements (is someone crouching to attack?), interactions between people and objects (is someone picking up a weapon?), and background context (where is this happening?). These factors interact in complex ways—the same body posture is threat in one context, normal in another.
749.ap: DeepSVU uses a unified approach called UPRM (Unified Physical-world Regularized Mixture of Experts). It combines human behavior analysis, object interaction detection, and scene context into a single representation. A Mixture of Experts component learns to decide which information is most important for each video segment—sometimes body language dominates, sometimes object interaction is key. A trade-off regularizer balances these factors so the model doesn't just latch onto one signal.
749.ww: Modeling physical-world information (what people and objects actually do) rather than just abstract features helps because causality is visible in the real world. When you know a person's posture, what they're holding, and where they are, you can infer intent. The mixture-of-experts design allows flexibility: a mugging looks different from a medical emergency, and the model learns which physical signals matter for each.
749.po: The system not only flags dangerous video segments but explains them: 'this frame is dangerous because [person A] is [action] [object B] in [location].' This enables faster human review and better security response. On security video benchmarks, it outperforms methods that just detect anomalies, providing the explainability that human operators need to act quickly and correctly.
